title: TCP: Handshake, Reliability and Teardown
objectives: Trace the three-way handshake and the close
Explain sequence numbers, acknowledgements and retransmission
Count round trips before the first response byte

cards.title: A reliable stream over unreliable packets
cards.body: IP may drop, duplicate or reorder packets. TCP numbers every byte it sends, has the receiver acknowledge what arrived, and resends what was not acknowledged, so the application reads one ordered stream with no gaps.

cards.title: Worked example: time to the first byte
cards.body: Connection setup costs round trips before any data moves.
steps: Assume: 80 ms round trip time (RTT), plain HTTP, no TLS
SYN out and SYN-ACK back: 1 RTT = 80 ms
The final ACK travels with the request; the response returns: 1 more RTT
Server processing ignored
cards.note: Result. About 160 ms before the first response byte on a new connection, against 80 ms on a reused one. Adding TLS 1.3 adds one more round trip, which is why connection reuse matters on long paths.

cards.title: The three-way handshake
cards.body: Both sides pick a starting sequence number and confirm the other’s.
steps: Client sends SYN with its initial sequence number
Server replies SYN-ACK: its own number, acknowledging the client’s
Client sends ACK; the connection is established
Data can now flow both ways
Initial numbers are chosen unpredictably so attackers cannot inject segments

cards.title: Closing and TIME_WAIT
cards.body: Each direction is closed separately with FIN and ACK. The side that closes first then waits in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime, so stray old segments cannot be mistaken for a new connection using the same addresses and ports. A RST aborts a connection immediately.

cards.title: Trap: treating “sent” as “delivered”
cards.body: A successful write only means the data reached your own operating system’s send buffer. If the peer crashes, TCP cannot tell you which bytes the application on the other side processed. Applications that need certainty must acknowledge at their own level, for example with response codes or idempotent retries.

cards.title: Edge case: running out of ports for outbound connections
cards.body: The side that closes a TCP connection first keeps it in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime. A client opening many short connections to one destination can use up its ephemeral ports (Linux’s default range, 32768–60999, is about 28,000 ports) and new connections fail. Reuse connections with keep-alive or pooling rather than tuning TIME_WAIT away.

questions.prompt: A capture shows the server’s SYN-ACK with seq=5000 and ack=1001. What does it tell you?

choices.label: Server starts at 5000; it got the SYN numbered 1000
The server has received 1,001 bytes of data
The client’s data must start at byte 5000
The server is about to send 1,001 bytes

questions.explanation: A SYN uses up one sequence number, so ack=1001 acknowledges the client’s SYN, whose initial number was 1000; seq=5000 is the server’s own starting number. No data has moved yet, the client’s data continues from 1001, not 5000, and the ack field says what was received, not what will be sent.

questions.prompt: The sender receives three duplicate ACKs for the same sequence number. What does it do?

choices.label: Doubles its sending rate to catch up quickly
Waits for the retransmission timer to expire first
Resends the missing segment at once (fast retransmit)
Closes the connection immediately with a RST

questions.explanation: Three duplicate ACKs say one segment is missing while later ones arrived, so the sender resends it at once (fast retransmit) instead of waiting for the much longer timer, and it also reduces its window. It does not speed up, and it does not reset the connection.

questions.prompt: Which side of a connection enters TIME_WAIT?

choices.label: The side that closes first
Neither, unless an error occurs
Always the client
Always the server

questions.explanation: The active closer waits 2×MSL before reusing the address and port pair. Who initiated the connection does not matter, only who sent the first FIN; the passive closer goes to CLOSED as soon as its own FIN is acknowledged; and TIME_WAIT is part of every normal close, not an error path.

questions.prompt: Your write call returned success, then the peer machine lost power. What do you know?

choices.label: Only that the data reached your local send buffer
That the peer application processed the data
That the peer’s operating system acknowledged it
That the data was written to the peer’s disk

questions.explanation: A successful write means only that the bytes reached your own kernel’s send buffer. The peer’s operating system may never have received them, let alone the application processing them or writing them to disk; only an application-level reply proves that.

questions.prompt: Order the messages to open a connection and send a request.

items.label: Client sends ACK (often with the request)
Client acknowledges the response
Client sends SYN
Server sends the response data
Server sends SYN-ACK

questions.explanation: Three-way handshake, then data and acknowledgements.

questions.prompt: RTT is 50 ms. On a new plain TCP connection (no TLS), about how many milliseconds until the first response byte, ignoring server time?
assumptions: One RTT for request and response
questions.explanation: Design implication: half of that is connection setup, so keeping connections open and reusing them halves the delay for every later request.

flashcards.back: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK.
Three duplicate ACKs.
The side that closes first, for 2 × MSL.

mechanism.title: What TCP does to make a stream reliable
steps: TCP numbers bytes, not packets. Each segment carries the sequence number of its first byte, and the receiver acknowledges the next byte it expects. Acknowledgements are cumulative: an ACK for byte 5,001 says everything before it has arrived.
The handshake synchronises the starting numbers. Initial sequence numbers are chosen unpredictably (RFC 9293 discusses the generator) so an off-path attacker cannot guess them and inject data.

Loss is detected two ways. A retransmission timer, derived from measured round-trip times, fires when an ACK is overdue (RFC 6298 recommends an initial value of 1 second and doubling on each timeout). Three duplicate ACKs trigger a fast retransmit sooner.

The receiver buffers out-of-order segments and hands bytes to the application only in order. One lost segment therefore delays everything behind it, which is head-of-line blocking at the transport layer.

Closing is a half-close per direction: FIN says “I will send no more”, and the other side can keep sending until it sends its own FIN. RST aborts immediately, for example when a segment arrives for a port with no listener.

TIME_WAIT lasts 2 × MSL (maximum segment lifetime) on the active closer. Servers that close many short connections can accumulate thousands of TIME_WAIT entries; reusing connections avoids most of them.

useWhen: Use TCP when you need every byte, in order, and can accept head-of-line blocking.
Reuse connections (keep-alive, pooling) to avoid paying the handshake on every request.
avoidWhen: Avoid treating a successful write as proof the peer processed the data.
Avoid opening a new connection per small request on long-RTT paths.

rows: At least the RTO, often hundreds of ms

numbers.title: Why a tail loss hurts more than a middle loss
assumptions: RTT 100 ms; retransmission timeout 300 ms (illustrative: Linux uses a 200 ms minimum, while RFC 6298 recommends 1 s, which makes a tail loss even slower)
steps: Loss of segment 3: segments 4 to 10 arrive and produce duplicate ACKs, so fast retransmit resends segment 3 after about one RTT: roughly 100 ms extra.
Loss of segment 10 (the last): no later segments arrive, so no duplicate ACKs, and the sender waits for the 300 ms timer.
The same single loss costs about three times longer at the tail under these assumptions.
Modern stacks add probes for tail loss, but the principle explains why short responses on lossy links see long, uneven delays.
numbers.result: Where a loss happens matters as much as whether it happens; tail losses wait on timers.

india.title: Retransmission timers in RFC 6298
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 6298 specifies how TCP computes its retransmission timeout from smoothed RTT measurements and their variation, with a minimum of 1 second recommended and exponential backoff after each timeout. RFC 5681 defines fast retransmit on the third duplicate ACK. Together they explain why a lost packet can cost anything from one round trip to several seconds.

pitfalls.trap: “TCP guarantees the server got my request.”
pitfalls.say: “It guarantees ordered delivery while the connection lives; to know it was processed I need an application-level response.”

pitfalls.trap: “Each request opens a fresh connection; it’s simpler.”
pitfalls.say: “That costs a round trip, or more with TLS, every time; I’d reuse connections.”

takeaways: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK opens a connection in one round trip.
Sequence numbers and cumulative ACKs give an ordered stream; losses are resent.
Fast retransmit needs later segments; tail losses wait for the timer.
The active closer holds TIME_WAIT for 2 × MSL.

interactive.title: Which loss is slower?
interactive.prompt: A server sends a 10-segment response over a path with a 100 ms RTT. In one case segment 3 is lost; in another, segment 10 is lost. Which case usually delays the response more?

choices.label: Losing segment 10, the last one
choices.feedback: Right: with nothing after it there are no duplicate ACKs, so the sender waits for its retransmission timer.

choices.label: Losing segment 3
choices.feedback: Later segments trigger duplicate ACKs and a fast retransmit after about one RTT.

choices.label: Both cost exactly the same
choices.feedback: Detection differs: duplicate ACKs versus waiting for a timer.

interactive.reveal: TCP recovers faster from losses it can detect through later data. Tail losses are why short transfers on lossy links feel slow.

seeAlso.why: Choosing TCP or UDP in a system design
Why the handshake round trips dominate small transfers

title: TCP Flow Control and Congestion Control
objectives: Tell flow control from congestion control
Compute the window needed to fill a link (bandwidth-delay product)
Explain slow start and the response to loss

cards.title: Two brakes on the sender
cards.body: A TCP sender may have only so many unacknowledged bytes in flight. The receiver advertises how much buffer it has (the receive window: flow control). The sender also keeps its own estimate of what the network can carry (the congestion window: congestion control). It sends no more than the smaller of the two.

cards.title: Worked example: why one download is slow on a fast link
cards.body: With a fixed window, throughput is capped at window ÷ round-trip time, whatever the link speed.
steps: Assume: 100 Mbit/s link, 50 ms RTT, window stuck at 64 KiB (65,536 bytes)
Throughput ≤ 65,536 × 8 bits ÷ 0.05 s ≈ 10.5 Mbit/s
To fill the link: 100,000,000 ÷ 8 × 0.05 = 625,000 bytes ≈ 610 KiB in flight
That needs the window scaling option, since the basic header field stops at 65,535 bytes
cards.note: Result. One connection uses about a tenth of the link under these assumptions. Larger buffers with window scaling, or several connections, are needed to fill long, fast paths.

cards.title: Slow start, then careful growth
cards.body: The congestion window grows quickly at first and then cautiously.
steps: Start with a small initial window (up to about 10 segments is common)
Slow start: grow by about one segment per ACK, roughly doubling each RTT
Reach the slow-start threshold: switch to congestion avoidance
Congestion avoidance: add about one segment per RTT
On loss: cut the window (roughly in half) and continue

cards.title: The bandwidth-delay product
cards.body: Bandwidth × round-trip time is how many bytes must be in flight to keep a path busy. A 1 Gbit/s link with a 100 ms RTT needs 12.5 MB in flight. If buffers or windows are smaller than that, the sender sits idle waiting for acknowledgements.

cards.title: Trap: blaming the link for a short-transfer slowdown
cards.body: Small responses often finish while the connection is still in slow start, so they never reach full speed. A faster link barely helps them; fewer round trips (connection reuse, fewer sequential requests, a closer server) help much more.

cards.title: Edge case: bufferbloat
cards.body: Loss-based congestion control keeps increasing its window until packets drop, so a router with a very large buffer fills it before loss tells the sender to slow down. Every packet then waits in that queue, and latency on a busy home link can grow by hundreds of milliseconds. Active queue management in routers (for example CoDel) and delay-based algorithms such as BBR reduce it.

questions.prompt: A phone downloads from a fast server, but the app reading the data is slow and the phone’s receive buffer is full. What makes the server pause?

choices.label: Packets expire as their IP time to live runs out
The server’s congestion window shrinks after loss
The phone repeats the three-way handshake
The phone advertises a receive window of zero

questions.explanation: This is flow control: the receiver advertises how much buffer is free, and at zero the sender stops, probing until space opens. The congestion window reacts to the network, not to a slow receiver; the time to live limits hops; and the handshake happens once per connection.

questions.prompt: In classic TCP congestion control, what happens when loss is detected by duplicate ACKs?

choices.label: The connection is reset and reopened
The congestion window is cut, roughly in half
The window doubles to recover faster
The receiver shrinks its buffer

questions.explanation: Duplicate ACKs are a congestion signal, so classic TCP halves its window (multiplicative decrease) and carries on rather than resetting. Doubling would add to the congestion, and the receiver’s buffer is a flow-control matter that has nothing to do with loss.

questions.prompt: A 1 Gbit/s path has a 100 ms RTT. About how much data must be in flight to fill it?

choices.label: 125 MB
125 KB

questions.explanation: 10⁹ bits/s × 0.1 s = 10⁸ bits = 12.5 MB. 125 MB multiplies by a full second, and 1.25 MB or 125 KB would leave the link idle for most of each round trip.

questions.prompt: A server in Mumbai sends a backup to Frankfurt over a 1 Gbit/s path with a 120 ms RTT. Window scaling is turned off. What is the most it can achieve?

choices.label: About 4.4 Mbit/s
About 44 Mbit/s
About 440 Mbit/s
The full 1 Gbit/s

questions.explanation: Without scaling the window field stops at 65,535 bytes, and throughput ≤ window ÷ RTT = 65,535 × 8 ÷ 0.12 s ≈ 4.4 Mbit/s, under 1% of the link. Filling it needs about 15 MB in flight (10⁹ ÷ 8 × 0.12 s), which only window scaling allows.

questions.prompt: Order a new connection’s congestion window behaviour.

items.label: Pass the slow-start threshold
Grow rapidly in slow start
Grow by about one segment per RTT
Start at a small initial window
Cut the window when loss is detected

questions.explanation: Exponential growth, then linear, then a cut on loss.

questions.prompt: A connection’s window is 125,000 bytes and the RTT is 100 ms. What is its maximum throughput in Mbit/s?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: doubling the RTT to 200 ms would halve this, so distant users see slow single downloads even on fast links unless windows grow.

flashcards.back: Flow control protects the receiver; congestion control protects the network.
Bandwidth × RTT: bytes needed in flight to fill a path.

flashcards.front: Max throughput with a fixed window?
flashcards.back: Window ÷ RTT.

sources.title: RFC 7323: TCP Extensions for High Performance
RFC 9438: CUBIC for Fast and Long-Distance Networks

mechanism.title: How TCP decides how fast to send
steps: Every TCP segment carries a receive window: the free space in the receiver’s buffer. The sender never has more unacknowledged bytes outstanding than this. If the receiving application stops reading, the window shrinks to zero and the sender pauses.

The basic window field is 16 bits, so it tops out at 65,535 bytes. The window scale option (RFC 7323), agreed in the handshake, multiplies it by a power of two so windows can reach around a gigabyte, which long, fast paths need.

Congestion control is the sender’s own limit, the congestion window. RFC 5681 describes the classic scheme: slow start roughly doubles the window each round trip until a threshold or a loss; congestion avoidance then grows it by about one segment per round trip; a loss cuts it.

RFC 6928 allows an initial window of up to 10 segments (about 14 KB), and many stacks use that. Most systems now default to CUBIC (RFC 9438), which grows the window as a function of time since the last loss so it fills fast links faster; other algorithms such as BBR model bandwidth and delay instead of reacting only to loss.

Throughput of one connection is bounded by min(receive window, congestion window) ÷ RTT. Halving the RTT doubles the ceiling, which is a major reason CDNs and nearby servers make transfers faster even when bandwidth is unchanged.

Queues in routers absorb bursts, but oversized buffers add delay without adding throughput (“bufferbloat”). Active queue management drops or marks packets early so senders slow down before latency climbs.

useWhen: Raise buffer limits and keep window scaling on for high-bandwidth, long-RTT transfers.
Reuse warm connections so later requests skip slow start.
avoidWhen: Avoid expecting a single connection to fill a long, fast path with small windows.
Avoid opening many parallel connections to “beat” congestion control; it is unfair to other traffic and adds load.

numbers.title: How long slow start takes to reach full speed
assumptions: Path: 100 Mbit/s, 50 ms RTT, so about 625,000 bytes (≈ 430 segments of 1,460 bytes) needed in flight
Initial window 10 segments, doubling each RTT, no loss
steps: RTT 1: 10 segments; RTT 2: 20; RTT 3: 40; RTT 4: 80; RTT 5: 160; RTT 6: 320; RTT 7: 640.
The window passes about 430 segments during the seventh round trip.
That is roughly 7 × 50 ms = 350 ms before the connection can use the whole link.
Total sent by then: 10 + 20 + … + 320 = 630 segments, about 0.9 MB, so smaller responses finish before reaching full speed.
numbers.result: Responses under about a megabyte on this path are limited by round trips, not by the link; reuse and proximity help more than bandwidth.

india.title: Initial window and CUBIC in the RFCs
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 6928 records the move from an initial window of 2–4 segments to up to 10, based on measurements showing faster web page loads with little added loss. RFC 9438 documents CUBIC, which many operating systems use by default, designed so that long, fast paths recover their sending rate more quickly after a loss than classic additive increase allows.

pitfalls.trap: “We have a 1 Gbit/s link, so this download should be fast.”
pitfalls.say: “One connection is capped at window ÷ RTT; on a 100 ms path I’d check window scaling and buffer sizes.”

pitfalls.trap: “Bandwidth is the problem for our small API responses.”
pitfalls.say: “They finish during slow start; reducing round trips helps more than bandwidth.”

takeaways: The sender keeps in flight no more than the smaller of the receive and congestion windows.
Throughput ≤ window ÷ RTT; the bandwidth-delay product says how much is needed.
Slow start doubles per RTT; losses cut the window.
Short transfers are latency-bound; long ones need big windows.

interactive.title: Fill the pipe
interactive.prompt: A 100 Mbit/s path has a 50 ms round trip. Change the TCP window and see how much of the link one connection can use.
interactive.takeaway: Throughput rises in proportion to the window until it reaches about 610 KiB (bandwidth × delay), then the link is full. A 64 KiB window, the most possible without window scaling, uses only about a tenth of this link.

seeAlso.why: TCP versus UDP trade-offs in system design

title: UDP, Ports and Sockets
objectives: Explain what UDP does and does not do
Identify a connection by its addresses and ports
Estimate limits from ephemeral port ranges

cards.title: Ports pick the process, sockets are the handle
cards.body: An IP address gets a packet to a machine; a port number (0–65,535) gets it to a process. A socket is the operating system’s handle for one endpoint. A TCP connection is identified by four values: source address, source port, destination address and destination port.

cards.title: Worked example: running out of source ports
cards.body: Each outbound connection to the same server address and port needs a different local port.
steps: Assume: a proxy connects to one backend address and port, using the IANA ephemeral range 49,152–65,535
That range holds 65,535 − 49,152 + 1 = 16,384 ports
Each connection the proxy closes first keeps its port in TIME_WAIT for 60 s (Linux’s fixed value)
Sustainable new connections: 16,384 ÷ 60 ≈ 273 per second
cards.note: Result. Under these assumptions the proxy cannot open more than about 273 new connections a second to that backend. Operating systems choose their own ranges, but the fix is the same: reuse connections, or add backend addresses.

cards.title: One server port, many connections
cards.body: A listening socket accepts connections; each accepted connection gets its own socket.
steps: Server listens on 0.0.0.0:443
Client A connects from 198.51.100.4:50001
Client B connects from 198.51.100.4:50002 (same machine, new port)
Each pair forms a distinct four-tuple and a separate socket
The server port stays 443 for all of them

cards.title: UDP: just datagrams
cards.body: UDP adds an 8-byte header with ports, a length and a checksum. There is no handshake, ordering, retransmission or congestion control. Each send is one datagram that arrives whole or not at all. DNS, voice and video calls, games and QUIC (which builds its own reliability) use it.

cards.title: Trap: sending large UDP datagrams
cards.body: A datagram bigger than the path MTU is fragmented at the IP layer, and losing any fragment loses the whole datagram; many networks drop fragments outright. Keep datagrams under the path MTU (about 1,200 bytes is a common safe size), and add your own pacing so you do not flood the network.

cards.title: Edge case: UDP reflection and amplification
cards.body: UDP has no handshake, so an attacker can forge the source address. Small queries to open DNS resolvers or other UDP services that send large replies are reflected at the forged victim, multiplying the attack traffic. Services on UDP should avoid replies much larger than requests to unverified clients, and networks should drop packets with spoofed sources.

questions.prompt: A server on port 443 has 10,000 open connections. How does it tell them apart?

choices.label: Each connection gets a different server port
By the order in which packets arrive
By the client address and port in each four-tuple
By a session id in the IP header

questions.explanation: A TCP connection is identified by four values: client address, client port, server address and server port. All 10,000 share the server’s address and port 443, but each client address and port pair is different. The server does not hand out new ports per connection, arrival order identifies nothing, and IP headers carry no session id.

questions.prompt: A team ships device telemetry over UDP. On a congested link, 2% of datagrams vanish and some arrive out of order. What did UDP itself guarantee?

choices.label: Lost datagrams are resent after a short timeout
Datagrams are delivered in the order they were sent
Only ports and a checksum on what does arrive
The sender slows down when the link is congested

questions.explanation: UDP adds ports and a checksum to IP and nothing else: no retransmission, no ordering and no congestion control. The application must number its messages, tolerate loss or resend what matters, and pace itself, or use a protocol such as QUIC that builds those on top of UDP.

questions.prompt: A Linux service with default settings opens many short connections to one database address and port. New connections start failing at about 28,000 open sockets. What sets that number?

choices.label: TCP allows about 28,000 connections per server port
The OS ephemeral port range, 32,768–60,999
IANA caps each address at 28,000 connections
Ports above 49,152 are reserved for servers

questions.explanation: Each connection to the same destination needs a distinct local port, and Linux picks them from 32,768–60,999 by default: 28,232 ports. Closed connections also hold their port in TIME_WAIT for a while. Widen the range, add source addresses or reuse connections. The IANA dynamic range is 49,152–65,535 (RFC 6335), but that is advice, not a cap, and a server port has no such limit.

questions.prompt: A video call loses one packet. Why might the app prefer UDP to TCP here?

choices.label: UDP packets are encrypted by default on the internet
UDP retransmits lost packets faster than TCP does
TCP cannot carry real-time audio or video data
A late resend is useless, and TCP would stall later data behind it

questions.explanation: By the time a lost audio packet could be resent, its moment has passed, and TCP would hold back every later byte until the resend arrived, freezing the call. Over UDP the app plays the next packet and conceals the gap. UDP is not encrypted by itself (apps add DTLS or SRTP), it never retransmits, and TCP can carry media, just with stalls on loss.

questions.prompt: Order what a server does to handle TCP clients.

items.label: Listen for connections
Read and write on the accepted socket
Create a socket
Bind it to an address and port
Accept a connection, getting a new socket

questions.explanation: A server creates a socket, binds it to an address and port, marks it listening, and then accepts connections; each accept returns a new socket for that one client, which it reads and writes while the listening socket keeps accepting others.

questions.prompt: A client has 16,384 ephemeral ports for one destination, and each closed connection holds its port for 120 s. About how many new connections per second can it sustain?
questions.explanation: Design implication: a client that opens a new connection per request will hit this ceiling under load, so keep connections alive and reuse them.

flashcards.back: Source address and port plus destination address and port (and the protocol).
8 bytes.

sources.title: RFC 6335: IANA Procedures for Port Numbers
IANA Service Name and Port Number Registry

mechanism.title: How ports, sockets and datagrams work
steps: Port numbers are 16 bits. IANA divides them into well-known (0–1,023, such as 53 for DNS and 443 for HTTPS), registered (1,024–49,151) and dynamic or private (49,152–65,535). On many systems, binding to ports below 1,024 needs extra privileges.

A server creates a socket, binds it to an address and port, and listens. Each accepted connection gets a new socket, so one listening port serves any number of clients, limited by memory and file descriptors rather than ports.

A client usually lets the operating system pick a local ephemeral port. Because a connection is unique by its four-tuple, a client can have only as many simultaneous connections to one destination address and port as it has local ports, minus those still in TIME_WAIT.

UDP (RFC 768) sends independent datagrams with an 8-byte header. The checksum is optional over IPv4 and required over IPv6. There is no connection: a UDP socket can send to and receive from many peers.
Because UDP has no congestion control, RFC 8085 asks applications to provide their own: limit sending rates, back off on loss, and keep datagrams within the path MTU to avoid IP fragmentation.

QUIC runs over UDP and rebuilds what it needs (reliability per stream, congestion control, encryption) in user space. That avoids changes to operating system kernels and middleboxes that only understand TCP and UDP.

useWhen: Use UDP for small request–response exchanges (DNS) and real-time data where late is as bad as lost.
Reuse TCP connections to keep ephemeral port use low.
avoidWhen: Avoid UDP if you would end up re-implementing TCP badly.
Avoid UDP datagrams larger than the path MTU.

rows: Best effort, each datagram whole or lost

numbers.title: Connections a server can hold on one port
assumptions: Each client connection uses about 10 KB of kernel and application memory (illustrative)
8 GB of memory set aside for connections
steps: Ports are not the limit on the server: each connection differs by client address and port.
Memory: 8,000,000 KB ÷ 10 KB ≈ 800,000 connections.
File descriptor limits must also be raised to that order, since each socket uses one.
On the client side the limit is different: about 16,000–28,000 ephemeral ports per destination, depending on the system’s range.
numbers.result: Servers are limited by memory and descriptors; clients and proxies are limited by ephemeral ports per destination.

india.title: Port number ranges at IANA
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 6335 defines the three port ranges and the procedures IANA uses to assign service names and port numbers, which IANA publishes in its Service Name and Port Number Registry. It recommends that operating systems choose ephemeral ports from the dynamic range 49,152–65,535, though many systems use a wider range of their own choosing. RFC 8085 gives the guidelines for applications that use UDP.

pitfalls.trap: “Our server ran out of ports.”
pitfalls.say: “A server port serves unlimited four-tuples; I’d check file descriptors and memory, or ephemeral ports on the proxy side.”

pitfalls.trap: “UDP is faster, so let’s use it for our API.”
pitfalls.say: “UDP only removes the handshake and reliability; I’d use it only if I can handle loss, ordering and congestion myself.”

takeaways: A TCP connection is unique by its four-tuple.
One server port can serve any number of clients.
Clients and proxies are limited by ephemeral ports per destination.
UDP gives ports and a checksum, nothing else.

interactive.title: What runs out first?
interactive.prompt: A reverse proxy opens a new TCP connection to one backend address and port for every incoming request, and closes it afterwards. Traffic grows to several thousand requests per second. What fails first?

choices.label: The proxy runs out of local ephemeral ports to that backend
choices.feedback: Right: closed connections hold their ports in TIME_WAIT, so new connections run out of source ports.

choices.label: The backend runs out of ports on 8080
choices.feedback: A server port can serve any number of four-tuples.

choices.label: The backend’s IP address runs out of capacity
choices.feedback: Addresses do not have a connection limit; ports per tuple do.

interactive.reveal: Connection churn exhausts ephemeral ports on the side that opens connections. Keep-alive pools to the backend fix it.

seeAlso.why: TCP vs UDP for system design choices
Ports and sockets are what a connection pool holds open

title: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
objectives: Explain what changed in each HTTP version
Locate head-of-line blocking in each
Choose what to enable on a server and why

cards.title: Same meaning, different transport
cards.body: All three versions carry the same semantics: methods, status codes, headers and bodies. What changes is how messages are put on the wire: text over TCP (1.1), binary frames multiplexed over one TCP connection (2), and multiplexed streams over QUIC on UDP (3).

cards.title: Worked example: 36 small files on a slow path
cards.body: A simplified model shows why multiplexing mattered for pages with many assets.
steps: Assume: 36 small files, 50 ms RTT, each request takes about one RTT, bandwidth not the limit
HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections: 36 ÷ 6 = 6 rounds × 50 ms = 300 ms
HTTP/2 on one connection: all 36 requests sent at once, about 1 round: 50 ms
Connection setup is extra in both cases
cards.note: Result. About 300 ms against 50 ms in this simplified model. Real pages differ (dependencies, bandwidth, server time), but cutting rounds of requests is the main gain.

cards.title: Head-of-line blocking at each version
cards.body: Each version moved the bottleneck lower down.
steps: HTTP/1.1: one response at a time per connection, so a slow response blocks the next
HTTP/2: many streams share one connection, so a slow response no longer blocks others
But one lost TCP packet stalls every stream until it is resent
HTTP/3: QUIC streams are independent, so a loss stalls only its own stream
Ordering is still kept within each stream

cards.title: Headers and connection set-up
cards.body: HTTP/2 compresses headers with HPACK and HTTP/3 with QPACK, which matters when many requests repeat the same cookies. HTTP/3 combines the transport and TLS 1.3 handshakes, so a new connection needs one round trip instead of two, and QUIC connection ids let a phone keep its connection when it switches from Wi-Fi to mobile data.

cards.title: Trap: bundling everything for HTTP/2
cards.body: Under HTTP/1.1, joining files and spreading assets across many host names reduced request rounds. With HTTP/2 and 3, extra host names prevent connection reuse and huge bundles hurt caching, since one changed line invalidates the whole file. Revisit those habits rather than keep them.

cards.title: Edge case: one HTTP/2 connection used for two host names
cards.body: Browsers may reuse an existing HTTP/2 connection for another host name when the certificate covers it and the name resolves to the same address (connection coalescing). If that server is not configured for the second name, it should answer 421 Misdirected Request so the browser retries on a new connection; servers that answer with the wrong site instead cause confusing bugs.

questions.prompt: Over HTTP/2 on a lossy network, one TCP packet is lost. What happens?

choices.label: The connection switches to HTTP/1.1
All streams on the connection wait until it is resent
The lost data is simply skipped
Only the stream that owned the packet waits

questions.explanation: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, and TCP hands bytes to the application only in order. A lost packet holds back all later bytes, from every stream, until it is retransmitted. The connection does not downgrade or skip data. HTTP/3 fixes this because QUIC orders bytes per stream.

questions.prompt: A corporate firewall blocks all outbound UDP except DNS. What happens to HTTP/3 for its users?

choices.label: Pages fail until the firewall allows UDP
HTTP/3 switches to running over TCP
Browsers fall back to HTTP/2 or 1.1 over TCP
Only the first request of each page uses HTTP/3

questions.explanation: HTTP/3 runs on QUIC, which runs over UDP (RFC 9114, RFC 9000), so with UDP blocked the QUIC attempt fails and browsers keep using the TCP connection with HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1. Nothing breaks, it is just slower on lossy links. HTTP/3 has no TCP mode, and browsers usually learn about HTTP/3 from a TCP response first anyway.

questions.prompt: Why did browsers open about six connections per host with HTTP/1.1?

choices.label: TLS only allowed six sessions per certificate
Servers refused to accept more than one request each
Each connection handles one response at a time
The HTTP/1.1 specification required exactly six

questions.explanation: HTTP/1.1 carries one request and response at a time per connection (pipelining was rarely usable), so browsers opened several connections, by convention about six per host, to fetch in parallel. No TLS or server rule set that number, and the specification never required six.

questions.prompt: A mobile user switches from Wi-Fi to cellular mid-download. Which version can keep the same connection?

choices.label: HTTP/3, because QUIC connections are identified by connection ids
HTTP/1.1, because its messages are plain text
None of them; every version must reconnect
HTTP/2, because it multiplexes many streams

questions.explanation: A TCP connection is tied to its four-tuple, so a new IP address after switching networks means a new connection for HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2. QUIC identifies connections by connection ids, so HTTP/3 can migrate to the new path and carry on. Multiplexing and plain text do not survive an address change.

questions.prompt: Order how a browser starts using HTTP/3 with a server it has not used before.

items.label: Connect over TCP and TLS and make the first request
Try a QUIC connection to the same server
Send later requests over HTTP/3 if QUIC works, otherwise stay on TCP
Receive a response advertising HTTP/3 (Alt-Svc header)

questions.explanation: Discovery happens over TCP first (or through DNS HTTPS records), with a fallback if UDP is blocked.

questions.prompt: A page needs 48 small files over HTTP/1.1 with 6 connections, 25 ms RTT, one RTT per request. About how many milliseconds of request rounds?
assumptions: Each connection fetches one file per round
questions.explanation: Sanity check: multiplexing the same files on one HTTP/2 connection is closer to a single 25 ms round, which is why fewer, sequential request chains matter more than file count today.

flashcards.back: Binary framing, multiplexed streams on one connection, header compression.
Transport head-of-line blocking, by using independent QUIC streams.

flashcards.front: What stays the same across versions?
flashcards.back: Semantics: methods, status codes, headers.

mechanism.title: What each version changed on the wire
steps: HTTP semantics are defined once, in RFC 9110, and shared by every version. That is why an application can move from HTTP/1.1 to 3 without changing routes, methods or status codes; proxies and servers translate between versions.

HTTP/1.1 (RFC 9112) sends text messages over TCP. Persistent connections avoid a handshake per request, but a connection carries one response at a time. Pipelining (sending several requests without waiting) was rarely usable in practice, so clients opened several connections per host instead.

HTTP/2 (RFC 9113) splits messages into binary frames tagged with a stream id, so many requests and responses interleave on one TCP connection. HPACK compresses repeated headers. Servers need fewer connections and clients avoid the per-connection limit.

HTTP/2’s weakness is below it: TCP delivers bytes in order, so a lost packet holds back data for every stream until retransmission. On lossy networks this can make HTTP/2 no faster than several HTTP/1.1 connections.

HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) runs over QUIC (RFC 9000), which provides streams, reliability and congestion control over UDP with TLS 1.3 built in. Loss affects only the stream it belongs to, new connections take one round trip, and resumed ones can send early data immediately.
Clients discover HTTP/3 through the Alt-Svc response header or DNS HTTPS records, then try QUIC and fall back to TCP if UDP is blocked. Servers usually offer all three versions at once.

useWhen: Enable HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 at the edge (load balancer or CDN) for browser traffic.
Prefer HTTP/3 where users are on mobile or lossy networks.
avoidWhen: Avoid domain sharding and giant bundles designed for HTTP/1.1 limits.
Avoid assuming UDP is always allowed; keep a TCP fallback.

numbers.title: Handshake round trips before the first request
steps: HTTP/1.1 or 2 over TCP and TLS 1.3: 1 RTT (TCP) + 1 RTT (TLS) = 160 ms before the request is sent.
With TLS 1.2: 1 + 2 = 3 RTT = 240 ms.
HTTP/3 over QUIC: transport and TLS combined in 1 RTT = 80 ms.
With resumption, QUIC can send the request in its first flight (0-RTT), but only for requests safe to replay.
numbers.result: On long paths, handshake round trips are a large share of the first request’s time, and HTTP/3 removes one of them.

india.title: The HTTP specifications today
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: In 2022 the IETF republished HTTP as a set: RFC 9110 for shared semantics, RFC 9111 for caching, and RFC 9112, 9113 and 9114 for the three wire formats. MDN’s “Evolution of HTTP” gives the history from HTTP/0.9, and RFC 9000 defines QUIC, the transport HTTP/3 depends on. RFC 9113 also deprecates the stream priority scheme of the original HTTP/2 specification, which was rarely implemented consistently, a reminder that protocol features are judged by deployment experience.

pitfalls.trap: “HTTP/2 fixed head-of-line blocking.”
pitfalls.say: “It fixed it at the HTTP layer; TCP still blocks all streams on a loss, which HTTP/3 fixes.”

pitfalls.trap: “Moving to HTTP/3 means changing our API.”
pitfalls.say: “Semantics are the same in every version; it is a server and edge configuration change.”

takeaways: All versions share the same semantics (RFC 9110).
HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection.
TCP loss still blocks every HTTP/2 stream; QUIC limits it to one.
HTTP/3 saves a handshake round trip and survives network changes.

interactive.title: Which version helps most?
interactive.prompt: Your users are mostly on mobile networks with frequent packet loss, loading many small API responses at once. Which change is likely to help most?

choices.label: Enable HTTP/3 at the edge
choices.feedback: Right: losses stall only one QUIC stream, and setup takes fewer round trips.

choices.label: Move from HTTP/2 back to HTTP/1.1
choices.feedback: More connections can help a little on loss, but you lose multiplexing and add handshakes.

choices.label: Shard requests across more host names
choices.feedback: That defeats connection reuse under HTTP/2 and 3.

interactive.reveal: On lossy networks, transport head-of-line blocking is the HTTP/2 weak spot. HTTP/3 keeps multiplexing and confines each loss to its own stream.

seeAlso.why: HTTP, HTTPS and TLS in system design
The protocol versions that carry these cache headers

title: The TLS Handshake
objectives: Trace a TLS 1.3 handshake and what each message proves
Explain how a certificate chain is checked
Know the risks of 0-RTT early data

cards.title: Three promises
cards.body: TLS gives a connection confidentiality (others cannot read it), integrity (others cannot change it undetected) and authentication (you are talking to the holder of the name’s certificate). The handshake agrees keys and proves the server’s identity before any application data is trusted.

cards.title: Worked example: round trips before the first byte
cards.body: Each protocol version changes how many round trips a new HTTPS connection costs.
steps: Assume: 100 ms RTT, new connection, no resumption, server time ignored
TCP handshake: 1 RTT
TLS 1.3: 1 RTT (TLS 1.2: 2 RTT)
HTTP request and response: 1 RTT
cards.note: Result. 300 ms with TLS 1.3 and 400 ms with TLS 1.2 before the first response byte. QUIC combines transport and TLS setup, bringing it to about 200 ms.

cards.title: A TLS 1.3 handshake
cards.body: The key exchange happens in the very first messages.
steps: ClientHello: supported versions and ciphers, a key share, and the server name (SNI)
ServerHello: chosen cipher and the server’s key share; both now derive keys
Server sends its certificate chain and a signature over the handshake (CertificateVerify)
Server Finished, then client Finished: both confirm they saw the same handshake
Encrypted application data flows

cards.title: Checking the certificate
cards.body: The client checks that the certificate names the host it asked for (in its subject alternative names), that it is within its validity dates, and that each certificate in the chain is signed by the next, ending at a root certificate authority the client already trusts. A signature from the server proves it holds the matching private key.

cards.title: Trap: sending non-idempotent requests as 0-RTT early data
cards.body: On a resumed connection, TLS 1.3 lets the client send data in its first flight. An attacker who records that flight can replay it, and the server may process it twice. Servers should accept early data only for requests that are safe to repeat, such as GETs without side effects.

cards.title: Edge case: the host name is visible in the handshake
cards.body: TLS encrypts the request, but the server name is sent in clear in the ClientHello’s SNI extension so the server can pick a certificate. Networks can therefore see, and filter on, which site you are reaching. Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) is the newer extension that hides it, where both sides support it.

questions.prompt: Users in Sydney reach your Mumbai servers over a round trip of about 150 ms. Moving from TLS 1.2 to TLS 1.3 saves how much on each new connection?

choices.label: Nothing: both need two round trips
About 150 ms, one round trip
About 300 ms, two round trips
About 15 ms of encryption work

questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 sends key shares in its first messages, so its handshake takes one round trip instead of TLS 1.2’s two: about 150 ms saved per new connection. It cannot save two, because TLS 1.3 still needs one, and encryption CPU time is tiny next to a 150 ms trip. Resumption with 0-RTT saves more, but only for replay-safe requests.

questions.prompt: A certificate is valid and signed by a trusted CA but issued for shop.example.com. The browser is connecting to pay.example.com. What happens?

choices.label: It succeeds because the CA is trusted
It falls back to unencrypted HTTP
It succeeds because the domains share example.com
The connection fails the host name check

questions.explanation: The certificate must list pay.example.com in its subject alternative names, or carry a wildcard such as *.example.com that covers it. A trusted CA vouches only for the names it signed, sharing a parent domain grants nothing, and browsers do not fall back to plain HTTP.

questions.prompt: An attacker records a year of a bank’s TLS 1.3 traffic, then steals the server’s certificate private key. Which recorded sessions can they decrypt?

choices.label: None of them
All of them
Only those from the last 90 days
Only those that used 0-RTT

questions.explanation: TLS 1.3 key exchange is ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, so session keys were never derivable from the certificate key: forward secrecy. The stolen key lets the attacker impersonate the server from now on, not read the past. With TLS 1.2’s old RSA key exchange, every recorded session would fall; certificate lifetimes do not matter here, and early data is protected by resumption secrets, not the certificate key.

questions.prompt: Which request is safe to send as 0-RTT early data?

choices.label: DELETE of a user account
POST that places an order
GET for a public product page
POST that transfers money

questions.explanation: An attacker can replay early data, so only a request that is safe to repeat belongs there. Replaying a DELETE, an order or a transfer would repeat its side effect, which is why servers refuse or delay those in early data, for example with 425 Too Early.

questions.prompt: Order the TLS 1.3 handshake messages.

items.label: Server Finished
Client Finished, then application data
ClientHello with a key share
Server certificate and CertificateVerify
ServerHello with its key share

questions.explanation: Keys are derived after the hellos; the rest of the handshake is already encrypted.

questions.prompt: RTT is 40 ms. On a new connection with TCP and TLS 1.2, about how many milliseconds until the first response byte, ignoring server time?
questions.explanation: Design implication: moving to TLS 1.3 saves one of those four round trips for every new connection, and connection reuse saves all of the setup.

flashcards.back: Confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.
One (zero for resumed early data).
It can be replayed.

mechanism.title: How TLS agrees keys and proves identity
steps: TLS sits between TCP (or QUIC) and the application. The handshake negotiates a version and cipher suite, runs a key exchange, and authenticates the server; afterwards records are encrypted and integrity-protected with symmetric keys.

In TLS 1.3 the client guesses a key exchange group and sends its key share in the ClientHello. The server replies with its own share, and both derive the same secrets using ephemeral Diffie–Hellman. Because the keys are temporary, a later leak of the server’s long-term key does not decrypt recorded sessions (forward secrecy).

Everything after the ServerHello is encrypted, including the certificate. The server proves it owns the certificate by signing a hash of the handshake (CertificateVerify), and both sides send a Finished message with a MAC over the whole handshake, so tampering with the negotiation is detected.

Certificate validation (RFC 5280) builds a chain from the server’s certificate through intermediates to a trusted root, checks signatures, validity periods and key usage, and checks revocation where configured. The host name must match a subject alternative name; RFC 6125 sets the matching rules, including limited wildcards.

The server name is sent in clear in the ClientHello (SNI) so one address can host many sites; Encrypted Client Hello is being deployed to hide it. Resumption uses a pre-shared key from an earlier session, which allows 0-RTT data, at the cost of possible replay.
Mutual TLS adds client certificates so the server also authenticates the client; it is common between services inside a system.

useWhen: Use TLS 1.3 (with 1.2 as a fallback) for all traffic, internal as well as external.
Use mutual TLS for service-to-service authentication where you control both ends.
avoidWhen: Avoid accepting 0-RTT early data for requests with side effects.
Avoid disabling certificate checks “just for testing” in code that may ship.

rows: Only with ephemeral key exchange ciphers
Removes old ciphers, encrypts more of the handshake
For the rest of the session

numbers.title: Handshake cost for users far from the server
assumptions: User 150 ms RTT from the origin; a CDN edge 20 ms away (illustrative)
steps: To the origin: TCP + TLS = 2 × 150 = 300 ms before the request is sent.
To the edge: 2 × 20 = 40 ms, and the edge keeps warm connections to the origin.
If the edge must fetch from the origin over a reused connection: 40 ms of setup + 20 ms for the request to the edge + 150 ms for the fetch = 210 ms, against 300 + 150 = 450 ms direct.
Terminating TLS near users saves the setup round trips even when the content itself comes from far away.
numbers.result: TLS setup is paid in round trips, so terminating it close to users is one of the largest latency wins for distant users.

india.title: What TLS 1.3 changed
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 8446 (2018) defines TLS 1.3. It removed static RSA and Diffie–Hellman key exchange, so every full handshake has forward secrecy; cut the full handshake to one round trip; encrypted the server certificate; and added 0-RTT data with an explicit section on replay risks. RFC 5280 defines the certificate format and path validation that clients still use to check identity.

pitfalls.trap: “HTTPS means the site is trustworthy.”
pitfalls.say: “It means the connection is private and the server holds a certificate for that name; it says nothing about the site’s intent.”

pitfalls.trap: “Turn on 0-RTT for everything.”
pitfalls.say: “Only for requests safe to replay, because early data can be captured and resent.”

takeaways: TLS gives confidentiality, integrity and server authentication.
A full TLS 1.3 handshake needs one round trip and always has forward secrecy (PSK-only resumption does not).
Clients check the chain, dates and host name.
Early (0-RTT) data can be replayed; keep it to safe requests.

interactive.title: Will this connection succeed?
interactive.prompt: A server presents a certificate for *.example.com, valid and signed by a trusted authority. The browser is connecting to api.eu.example.com.

choices.label: No: a wildcard covers only one label
choices.feedback: Right: *.example.com matches api.example.com but not api.eu.example.com.

choices.label: Yes: the wildcard covers every subdomain
choices.feedback: Wildcards match a single left-most label only.

choices.label: Yes, but only over TLS 1.2
choices.feedback: Name matching rules are the same in every TLS version.

interactive.reveal: Host name checks are strict: wildcards match exactly one label. Multi-level names need their own certificate entries.

TLS is what keeps a session cookie secret on the wire

title: Proxies and Forwarded Headers
objectives: Tell forward, reverse and intercepting proxies apart
Find the real client address safely
Explain how HTTPS passes through a forward proxy

cards.title: Someone in the middle, on purpose
cards.body: A proxy receives a request and makes it again on the client’s behalf. A forward proxy acts for clients (a company gateway); a reverse proxy acts for servers (a load balancer or CDN in front of your app). Each hop opens its own connection, so the server sees the proxy’s address, not the client’s.

cards.title: Worked example: reading X-Forwarded-For safely
cards.body: The header is a list, and only the parts added by proxies you control can be trusted.
steps: Assume: your app sits behind one trusted load balancer at 10.0.0.5
Request arrives from 10.0.0.5 with X-Forwarded-For: 203.0.113.7, 198.51.100.2
The load balancer appended 198.51.100.2, the address it saw
203.0.113.7 was already in the header when the request arrived, so the client may have written it
cards.note: Result. The client address is 198.51.100.2. Take the entry added by your outermost trusted proxy (counting from the right), never simply the first one, or anyone can spoof their address in logs and rate limits.

cards.title: HTTPS through a forward proxy
cards.body: The CONNECT method turns the proxy into a blind tunnel.
steps: Client sends CONNECT shop.example.com:443 to the proxy
Proxy opens a TCP connection to that host and replies 200
Client and server run TLS end to end through the tunnel
The proxy sees the host name and byte counts, not the content
Inspecting content needs a proxy certificate trusted by the client (interception)

cards.title: What reverse proxies do for you
cards.body: In front of an application, a reverse proxy terminates TLS, spreads requests over servers, caches responses, compresses, enforces limits and adds headers such as X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto or the standard Forwarded header. The application should trust those headers only from the proxy’s address.

cards.title: Trap: trusting forwarded headers from anyone
cards.body: If the application accepts X-Forwarded-For or X-Forwarded-Proto from any sender, a client reaching it directly, or through a proxy that passes headers along, can claim any address or scheme. Strip or overwrite these headers at the edge, and configure the app with the list of trusted proxy addresses.

cards.title: Edge case: client addresses through a layer-4 load balancer
cards.body: An L4 load balancer that terminates TCP cannot add an HTTP header, so the app sees the balancer’s address. The PROXY protocol solves this by sending a short header with the original client address at the start of the connection; the app must accept it only from the balancer, or anyone can claim any address.

questions.prompt: Which of these jobs needs a forward proxy rather than a reverse proxy?

choices.label: Filtering which outside sites employees can reach
Terminating TLS in front of your own API servers
Spreading requests across your app servers
Caching your product images near your users

questions.explanation: A forward proxy acts for clients going out, so it can filter and log the sites they visit. The other three act for your servers, in front of them: terminating TLS, balancing load and caching your content are reverse-proxy, load-balancer and CDN jobs.

questions.prompt: Behind one trusted load balancer, X-Forwarded-For is “192.0.2.44, 198.51.100.9”. Which is the client address?

choices.label: Neither address can be used
The load balancer’s own address

questions.explanation: Each proxy appends the address it received the connection from. Your one trusted load balancer appended 198.51.100.9, the address that connected to it, so that is the client. The leftmost entry arrived inside the request and could have been typed by anyone. The load balancer’s own address is not in the header; it is the TCP source the app sees.

questions.prompt: What can a forward proxy see of an HTTPS request sent through CONNECT?

choices.label: The request headers and the cookies sent
The response body returned by the server
The destination host and port, and how many bytes flow
The full URL path and its query string

questions.explanation: CONNECT names the host and port in the clear, and the proxy relays the bytes, so it sees the destination, timing and volume (and usually the name in the TLS handshake’s SNI). Everything inside TLS, the path, query string, headers, cookies and bodies, stays encrypted end to end unless the company installs its own certificate to intercept.

questions.prompt: Your app redirects to http:// URLs even though users connect with HTTPS to the load balancer. What is the likely fix?

choices.label: Trust X-Forwarded-Proto (or Forwarded) from the load balancer
Install the certificate on the app servers too
Lower the load balancer’s timeout
Turn on HTTP/2 between the balancer and the app

questions.explanation: The app only sees plain HTTP from the proxy unless it reads the forwarded scheme. Certificates on the app servers or HTTP/2 to the backend do not tell the app what the user used, and timeouts are unrelated to the scheme.

questions.prompt: Order an HTTPS request through a forward proxy.

items.label: Client runs the TLS handshake with the host through the tunnel
Proxy opens a TCP connection to the host
Encrypted HTTP requests flow through the tunnel
Proxy replies 200 Connection Established
Client sends CONNECT host:443 to the proxy

questions.explanation: The client asks the proxy to CONNECT to host:443, the proxy opens the TCP connection and replies 200, and from then on it only relays bytes: the client runs TLS with the real host through the tunnel and sends encrypted requests. Because TLS is end to end, the certificate checked is the host’s, not the proxy’s.

questions.prompt: A rate limiter keys on the client IP address. The app sits behind a CDN and then a load balancer.
constraints: Both the CDN and the load balancer are yours
Limits must apply per real client

approaches.label: Configure both proxies as trusted and take the address the CDN recorded
Use the TCP source address of the request

rationaleOptions.label: The leftmost entry is the original client
The socket address is the client
Skipping exactly your trusted hops lands on the real client
Entries added by your own proxies cannot be forged by clients

rationaleConflicts.r3: Clients can put anything there before the first proxy appends.
rationaleConflicts.r4: Behind proxies it is your load balancer, so every user shares one limit.

questions.explanation: The TCP source is your load balancer, so every client would share one limit, and the leftmost entry is whatever an attacker writes. Trusting exactly your CDN and load balancer, and reading X-Forwarded-For from the right past those hops, yields the address the CDN saw, which is the real client.

flashcards.back: Forward acts for clients; reverse acts for servers.
Opens a TCP tunnel through a proxy, used for HTTPS.
The one added by your outermost trusted proxy, counting from the right.

mechanism.title: What proxies change and how to recover the original request
steps: A proxy terminates one connection and opens another. The server therefore sees the proxy’s address as the source, the proxy’s TLS settings, and whatever headers the proxy chose to pass on. Information about the original request must be carried in headers.

The de facto headers are X-Forwarded-For (client address chain), X-Forwarded-Proto (original scheme) and X-Forwarded-Host. RFC 7239 standardised the same information in a single Forwarded header. Each proxy appends what it saw; nothing stops a client from sending a fake value first.

To find the client address, start from the socket’s peer address and walk the list from right to left, skipping addresses of proxies you trust. The first address not in your trusted list is the client. Most servers and frameworks have a “trusted proxies” setting that does exactly this.

A forward proxy handles plain HTTP requests by fetching the absolute URL itself, and HTTPS by the CONNECT method (RFC 9110), which creates a byte tunnel. The Via header records the proxies a message passed through.

Intercepting (TLS-inspecting) proxies decrypt traffic by presenting their own certificate, which clients accept only if the organisation installed the proxy’s root certificate. This breaks certificate pinning and end-to-end guarantees, so it is a policy decision, not a default.

Reverse proxies are where TLS termination, caching, compression, request size limits and routing usually live. Because they see every request, they are also the right place to set request ids and strip headers clients should not control.

useWhen: Use a reverse proxy to terminate TLS and apply limits before requests reach application code.
Configure an explicit trusted-proxy list wherever you read forwarded headers.
avoidWhen: Avoid taking the first X-Forwarded-For entry as the client address.
Avoid leaving app servers reachable directly, bypassing the proxy that sets headers.

numbers.title: How much a spoofable client address undermines a rate limit
assumptions: Limit: 100 requests per minute per client address (illustrative)
Attacker forges a random leftmost X-Forwarded-For value on each request
steps: If the app keys on the leftmost entry, every request looks like a new client, so the limit never triggers.
One attacker can send 10,000 requests a minute while appearing as 10,000 clients.
Keying on the address added by the trusted proxy collapses them back to one client, limited to 100 per minute.
If instead the app keyed on the socket address behind the proxy, all real users would share one limit of 100.
numbers.result: Picking the wrong address either lets attackers off or punishes everyone; the trusted-hop rule is what makes per-client limits work.

india.title: Forwarded headers in the standards
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: RFC 7239 defines the Forwarded header and notes that its values can be spoofed by clients and earlier proxies unless the receiver knows which proxies to trust. MDN’s X-Forwarded-For page gives the same advice for the de facto header: use the rightmost entries added by trusted proxies when the address matters for security, such as rate limiting.

pitfalls.trap: “The client IP is the first X-Forwarded-For value.”
pitfalls.say: “That value is client-supplied; I’d walk from the right, skipping only our trusted proxies.”

pitfalls.trap: “The proxy can read our users’ HTTPS traffic.”
pitfalls.say: “Not through CONNECT; only an intercepting proxy with a trusted root certificate can.”

takeaways: Forward proxies act for clients; reverse proxies act for servers.
Proxies append forwarded headers, and clients can forge earlier entries.
Find the client by skipping trusted hops from the right.
CONNECT tunnels HTTPS without exposing its content.

interactive.title: Who is the client?
interactive.prompt: Your app sits behind a CDN and a load balancer, both yours. A request arrives from the load balancer with X-Forwarded-For: 198.51.100.66, 203.0.113.50, 192.0.2.10, where 192.0.2.10 is a CDN edge address.

choices.feedback: Right: skip the load balancer (the socket address) and the CDN edge (192.0.2.10); the next entry is the client the CDN saw.
That entry was in the request before it reached your CDN, so the client could have written it.
That is your CDN edge, a trusted proxy, not the client.

interactive.reveal: Walk the list from the right and skip only proxies you run. The first address you do not trust is the client.

title: Latency vs Bandwidth
objectives: Separate latency, bandwidth and throughput
Estimate propagation delay from distance
Decide whether a transfer is latency-bound or bandwidth-bound

cards.title: How long vs how much
cards.body: Latency is how long one bit takes to arrive; bandwidth is how many bits per second a link can carry; throughput is what you actually achieve. A motorway analogy helps: latency is the drive time, bandwidth is the number of lanes. More lanes do not shorten the drive.

cards.title: Worked example: the speed of light sets a floor
cards.body: Light in optical fibre travels at roughly two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum, about 200,000 km per second.
steps: Assume: about 7,200 km great-circle distance between Mumbai and London
Round trip: 72 ms as an absolute minimum
Real cables are longer than the great circle, and routers and queues add more
cards.note: Result. No upgrade can bring this round trip below about 72 ms; measured values are higher. If a page needs ten sequential round trips to London, that alone is at least 0.7 s, which is why servers and caches near users matter.

cards.title: Is this transfer latency-bound?
cards.body: Compare the time spent waiting on round trips with the time spent pushing bytes.
steps: Count the round trips: connection setup plus each sequential request
Waiting time ≈ round trips × RTT
Sending time ≈ size × 8 ÷ bandwidth
Whichever is larger is what to attack first
Small API calls are almost always latency-bound

cards.title: Four kinds of delay
cards.body: Each hop adds propagation delay (distance), transmission delay (size ÷ link rate), processing delay (inspecting headers) and queueing delay (waiting behind other packets). Queueing is the one that varies, so it causes most jitter and most of the gap between average and tail latency.

cards.title: Trap: buying bandwidth for a latency problem
cards.body: If users wait on many small sequential requests, a faster link changes little. Measure where the time goes: reduce round trips, reuse connections, move content closer with a CDN, or send data in parallel. Upgrade bandwidth when large transfers dominate.

cards.title: Edge case: fast links still start slowly
cards.body: A new TCP connection begins with a small congestion window (commonly 10 segments, about 14 KB, per RFC 6928) and roughly doubles it each round trip. A 1 MB response on a fresh connection therefore needs several round trips however fast the link is, which is why connection reuse matters even on gigabit networks.

questions.prompt: A link is upgraded from 100 to 1,000 Mbit/s. What happens to the round-trip time for a tiny request?

choices.label: It stays about the same
It drops to a tenth
It doubles
It drops by about half

questions.explanation: Bandwidth does not change propagation delay, which dominates a tiny request. Serialisation time for a few hundred bytes was already microseconds, so neither halving nor a tenth is plausible, and nothing about a faster link doubles the delay.

questions.prompt: A game server in Mumbai serves players in Singapore, about 3,900 km away. What is the lowest possible round trip over fibre?

choices.label: About 13 ms
About 20 ms
About 39 ms
About 78 ms

questions.explanation: Fibre carries light at about 200,000 km/s, so one way takes 3,900 ÷ 200,000 ≈ 19.5 ms and a round trip at least 39 ms; real cable routes are longer, so measured values are higher. 13 ms uses the speed of light in a vacuum for one way, 20 ms forgets the return trip, and 78 ms counts the round trip twice.

questions.prompt: A page makes 12 sequential API calls of 2 KB each to a server 80 ms away. What helps most?

choices.label: A larger TCP receive buffer on the server side
Compressing each of the 2 KB JSON responses
Fewer sequential calls (batch them or run them in parallel)
A tenfold faster internet connection for users

questions.explanation: Twelve sequential calls wait 12 × 80 = 960 ms on round trips, while 24 KB takes about 4 ms to send even at 50 Mbit/s. Batching into one call, or running independent calls in parallel, removes most of the wait; a bigger buffer, compression or a faster link only shave those 4 ms.

questions.prompt: Pings to a server 1,000 km away range from 12 ms to 180 ms during the evening peak. Which delay is doing the varying?

choices.label: Transmission delay of the ping packets
Propagation delay along the fibre
Processing delay inside each router
Queueing delay in busy buffers

questions.explanation: The 1,000 km sets a floor of about 10 ms per round trip that does not move, and a small ping takes microseconds to transmit and process. What swings with evening load is time spent waiting in router and modem queues, which is why jitter and tail latency track congestion.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to decide what to optimise for a slow transfer.

items.label: Measure the RTT
Optimise whichever is larger
Count sequential round trips (setup and requests)
Compute sending time: size × 8 ÷ bandwidth
Compute waiting time: round trips × RTT

questions.explanation: Compare waiting with sending before choosing a fix.

questions.prompt: About how many milliseconds does light take to travel 2,000 km one way in optical fibre?
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a measured RTT of under 20 ms between two cities 2,000 km apart would be impossible over fibre, so a figure like that points to a nearer cache or a measurement error.

flashcards.back: Time for a bit to arrive vs bits per second the link carries.

flashcards.front: Light in fibre, rule of thumb?
flashcards.back: About 200,000 km/s, so 5 ms per 1,000 km one way.
Queueing delay.

sources.title: RFC 6349: Framework for TCP Throughput Testing

mechanism.title: Where network time goes
steps: Propagation delay is distance divided by signal speed. In fibre that is about 5 µs per kilometre, so 1 ms per 200 km one way. It is fixed by geography and cable routes; only moving endpoints closer reduces it.
Transmission (serialisation) delay is the time to put a packet on the wire: 1,500 bytes at 100 Mbit/s takes 0.12 ms, at 10 Mbit/s 1.2 ms. It matters on slow links and for large transfers.

Processing delay is the time a router or host takes to inspect and forward a packet, usually microseconds in hardware. Queueing delay is time spent waiting in buffers behind other traffic; it is zero on an idle link and large on a congested one.

Throughput for a single TCP connection is limited by window ÷ RTT (see the flow-control lesson), so long RTTs reduce throughput even on fast links. Measured throughput is usually below link bandwidth because of headers, retransmissions and slow start.

For a request that needs k sequential round trips and moves S bytes over bandwidth B, a rough model is time ≈ k × RTT + S × 8 ÷ B. Web pages and API calls are usually dominated by the first term; file downloads and video by the second.
Tail latency matters for users: if one page load makes 20 requests, it is likely to hit the slow tail of at least one of them. Reducing round trips helps averages and tails at once.

useWhen: Move content and TLS termination close to users when RTT dominates.
Increase bandwidth or compress when payload size dominates.
avoidWhen: Avoid chatty protocols with many sequential round trips over long distances.
Avoid judging network quality from averages alone; look at percentiles.

numbers.title: A 2 MB image vs an API call on the same path
assumptions: RTT 80 ms; bandwidth 50 Mbit/s; a warm connection (no setup)
API call: 1 round trip, 5 KB response; image: 1 round trip plus 2 MB of data
steps: API call: 80 ms waiting + 5,000 × 8 ÷ 50,000,000 s ≈ 0.8 ms sending: about 81 ms, almost all latency.
Image: 80 ms + 2,000,000 × 8 ÷ 50,000,000 s = 80 + 320 ms = 400 ms, mostly bandwidth.
Halving the RTT saves 40 ms on both; doubling bandwidth saves 0.4 ms on the API call and 160 ms on the image.
The best fix depends on which term dominates each request.
numbers.result: Small requests are latency-bound and big ones bandwidth-bound; measure which you have before choosing a fix.

india.title: Latency and bandwidth on MDN and web.dev
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: MDN’s glossary defines latency as the time between a request and the start of its response and bandwidth as the amount of data a network can carry per second, and its performance guides stress that latency, not bandwidth, usually limits web page loads. RFC 6349 explains why TCP throughput depends on the bandwidth-delay product and how to test it.

pitfalls.trap: “The site is slow; we need a faster connection.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d check whether it is latency-bound first; many small sequential requests do not speed up with bandwidth.”

pitfalls.trap: “Our London server is 20 ms from our users in India.”
pitfalls.say: “India–London is over 7,000 km, so the fibre round trip alone is about 70 ms and real paths are longer still, often well over 100 ms. A 20 ms figure means a nearer cache answered, or the measurement is wrong.”

takeaways: Latency is delay; bandwidth is capacity; throughput is what you achieve.
Light in fibre: about 5 ms per 1,000 km one way.
Time ≈ round trips × RTT + size × 8 ÷ bandwidth.
Fix the term that dominates.

interactive.title: Latency or bandwidth?
interactive.prompt: A warm connection makes 4 sequential round trips over an 80 ms path at 50 Mbit/s. Change the size of the data and see which part dominates.
interactive.takeaway: Up to about 2 MB the 320 ms of round trips dominates and more bandwidth barely helps. Above that, sending time takes over, and a faster link or a smaller payload pays off.
