title: What Happens When You Type a URL
objectives: Walk through a page load from URL to first response
Attach rough timings to each network step
Say which step each common optimisation removes

cards.title: One request, every layer
cards.body: Typing a URL and pressing Enter exercises most of this unit: parsing the URL, looking up the name, opening a connection, securing it, sending an HTTP request, and the server and browser work on either side. Each step either costs round trips or can be skipped with a cache.

cards.title: Worked example: a first visit at 50 ms RTT
cards.body: Adding up network steps shows where a first visit spends time before any HTML arrives.
steps: Assume: 50 ms RTT to the server; DNS answer from the recursive resolver in 30 ms; server takes 100 ms
DNS lookup: 30 ms
TCP handshake: 50 ms; TLS 1.3: 50 ms
Request and first response byte: 50 ms + 100 ms server time
cards.note: Result. About 280 ms to the first byte of HTML under these assumptions. On a repeat visit, a cached DNS answer and a reused connection remove 130 ms, leaving 150 ms.

cards.title: From Enter to first byte
cards.body: Most steps happen before the server is even reached.
steps: Parse the URL into scheme, host, port and path; apply HSTS to force HTTPS if known
Check the browser cache for a fresh copy
Resolve the host name (browser, operating system, then recursive resolver)
Open TCP and TLS, or QUIC for HTTP/3; check the certificate
Send the HTTP request; the server (often behind a CDN and load balancer) responds

cards.title: After the first byte
cards.body: The browser parses HTML as it streams in, finds CSS, scripts and images, and requests them, often on the same connection. Render-blocking CSS and scripts delay the first paint, so the network lessons and the frontend rendering lessons meet here.

cards.title: Trap: optimising the server when the network dominates
cards.body: If the server answers in 20 ms but users wait 600 ms, the time is in DNS, connection setup, distance and sequential resource requests. Browser timing data (navigation timing) splits the wait into these phases, so measure before tuning code.

cards.title: Edge case: broken IPv6 on the client’s network
cards.body: If a network advertises IPv6 but it does not actually work, a naive client would wait for an IPv6 connection to time out. Browsers use Happy Eyeballs (RFC 8305): they try IPv6 first and start IPv4 after a short delay if IPv6 has not connected, using whichever succeeds first, so a broken path costs about a quarter of a second (RFC 8305 recommends a 250 ms Connection Attempt Delay) instead of a long connection timeout.

questions.prompt: A user types example.com with no scheme. The site sent a Strict-Transport-Security header on an earlier visit. What does the browser do?

choices.label: Tries http:// and follows the redirect
Tries both schemes and keeps the faster
Uses https:// directly, skipping http://
Shows a warning before connecting

questions.explanation: HSTS tells the browser to use HTTPS for that host until max-age runs out, so it rewrites the URL to https:// before sending anything and skips the redirect round trip. Without HSTS it would try http:// first; browsers do not race the two schemes, and a known HSTS host gets no warning.

questions.prompt: A user reloads your page 10 minutes after the first visit. The DNS TTL is 300 s, the connection has closed and the HTML has Cache-Control: no-cache. What repeats?

choices.label: A DNS lookup, new TCP and TLS handshakes, then the request
Only the HTTP request; the rest is cached
Only TLS; DNS and TCP are still cached
Nothing; the HTML comes from the cache

questions.explanation: After 300 s the browser and operating system have dropped the name, so it is looked up again; a shared resolver may still answer quickly from its own cache if someone else asked recently, but the lookup happens. A closed connection must be reopened with TCP and TLS (a session ticket makes TLS cheaper, not free). Connections are not cached once closed, and no-cache means the browser must revalidate the HTML with the server before using its copy, often getting a 304.

questions.prompt: On a repeat visit a minute later, which steps are often skipped?

choices.label: The HTTP request itself
The DNS lookup and connection setup
Parsing the HTML
The certificate on every later request

questions.explanation: Cached DNS answers and kept-alive connections remove those round trips. The browser still requests the page, often as a quick revalidation, then parses the HTML and runs the page’s JavaScript again.

questions.prompt: Users far from your server wait 900 ms for the first byte; server time is 40 ms. What helps most?

choices.label: Serving from a CDN or region nearer the users
Increasing the server’s bandwidth
Adding more application servers
Rewriting the handler to save 20 ms

questions.explanation: With 40 ms of server time, most of the 900 ms is round trips over distance (DNS, TCP, TLS and the request), so an edge or a nearer region shortens every one of them. More bandwidth does not shorten a round trip, more servers help only when they are overloaded, and 20 ms saved in the handler is about 2% of the wait.

questions.prompt: Order what happens after pressing Enter on an uncached HTTPS site.

items.label: Look up the host name in DNS
Open a TCP connection
Parse the URL
Complete the TLS handshake
Send the HTTP request and receive the response
Parse the HTML and request its resources

questions.explanation: Name, connection, security, request, then rendering work.

questions.prompt: RTT 40 ms, DNS 20 ms, TCP and TLS 1.3 one RTT each, then one RTT for the request plus 60 ms server time. About how many milliseconds to the first byte?
assumptions: One RTT each for TCP, TLS and the request
questions.explanation: Design implication: 140 ms of the 200 is network, so a reused connection or an edge close to users does more than halving the server time.

flashcards.front: First network step for a new host?
flashcards.back: A DNS lookup.
The browser goes straight to HTTPS for that host.

flashcards.front: What do repeat visits often skip?
flashcards.back: DNS and connection setup.

mechanism.title: The full path of a page load
steps: URL parsing follows the WHATWG URL Standard: the browser splits the input into scheme, host, port, path, query and fragment, applies defaults (port 443 for https) and converts international host names. Without a scheme, browsers guess, and a known HSTS policy upgrades the request to HTTPS before anything is sent.

Before the network, the browser checks its HTTP cache. A fresh cached response is used directly; a stale one may be revalidated with a conditional request. Service workers, if registered, can intercept the request first.

Name resolution checks the browser’s DNS cache, then the operating system’s, then asks the recursive resolver, which may walk the DNS tree. Browsers often resolve names they expect to need early (DNS prefetch).

Connection setup: TCP handshake and TLS 1.3 (two round trips together), or QUIC for HTTP/3 (one). The certificate chain and host name are checked. Connections are kept open and reused for later requests to the same origin.

The request travels through any proxies, CDN edges and load balancers to an application server, which may read caches and databases before responding. Response headers set caching rules, cookies and security policies.

The browser streams the HTML into its parser, discovers CSS, scripts, fonts and images, requests them by priority, builds the DOM and CSSOM, lays out and paints. Navigation timing in the Performance API reports how long each phase took for real users.

useWhen: Use preconnect and DNS prefetch hints for third-party origins you know a page will need.
Use navigation timing from real users to see which phase dominates.
avoidWhen: Avoid redirect chains (http to https to www) that add round trips before the page starts.
Avoid many third-party origins, each needing its own DNS lookup and connection.

columns: Typical cost on a first visit

numbers.title: The cost of one redirect and one extra origin
assumptions: RTT 60 ms; first visit; TLS 1.3 over TCP (illustrative)
The page redirects http://example.com to https://www.example.com and loads fonts from another origin
steps: Redirect: the first connection and request (2 RTT for TCP and request on plain HTTP) only to learn the new URL: about 120 ms plus a DNS lookup for www.
Main page: TCP + TLS + request = 3 RTT = 180 ms.
Font origin: its own DNS lookup plus TCP + TLS = 2 RTT = 120 ms before the font request is even sent.
HSTS and a single origin (or preconnect) remove most of these 240 ms of setup.
numbers.result: Redirects and extra origins quietly add whole round trips; removing them often beats any server-side tuning.

india.title: URL parsing and navigation timing standards
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: The WHATWG URL Standard defines exactly how browsers parse what you type, and RFC 6797 defines HSTS, which lets a site tell browsers to use HTTPS only. The W3C Navigation Timing specification, documented on MDN, exposes timestamps for each phase (redirect, DNS, connect, TLS, request, response), which is how real-user monitoring tools build their waterfall charts.

pitfalls.trap: “The page is slow, so the server is slow.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d look at navigation timing; on a first visit DNS, connection setup and redirects can outweigh server time.”

pitfalls.trap: “Redirecting to HTTPS is free.”
pitfalls.say: “It costs a round trip or more on each first visit; HSTS lets the browser skip it.”

takeaways: A page load is parse, cache check, DNS, connect, TLS, request, then rendering.
First visits pay DNS and setup round trips; repeat visits often skip them.
Redirects and extra origins add whole round trips.
Measure phases with navigation timing before tuning.

interactive.title: Where did the time go?
interactive.prompt: Navigation timing for a slow first visit shows: redirect 130 ms, DNS 80 ms, connect plus TLS 160 ms, waiting for the first byte 70 ms, download 20 ms. What should you fix first?

choices.label: The redirect and connection setup
choices.feedback: Right: 370 of the 460 ms (redirect 130, DNS 80, connect and TLS 160) is setup before the real request; HSTS, no redirect, a warm DNS cache and a nearby edge cut most of it.

choices.label: The server’s response time
choices.feedback: Waiting for the first byte is only 70 ms here.

choices.label: The download size
choices.feedback: The download takes 20 ms.

interactive.reveal: Break the wait into phases. Most first-visit time here is spent before the request reaches the application.
